title: The Sun, Up Close
objective: After this level you can explain what powers the Sun and how dominant it is in the solar system.
summary: The Sun fuses hydrogen into helium, holds 99.8% of the solar system's mass, and is about 4.6 billion years old.

cards.headline: The Sun isn't on fire. It's doing something far stranger.
cards.body: It's easy to picture the Sun as a giant bonfire. But it has shone for billions of years, and it isn't burning in the everyday sense at all. Deep in its core, it's squeezing atoms together.

cards.headline: Nuclear fusion
cards.body: The Sun's core is about 15 million °C. At that heat, hydrogen atoms smash together so hard that they fuse into helium, and every fusion releases a tiny burst of energy. One burst is nothing, but the core does this an almost unimaginable number of times every second. Together, those bursts become all the light and warmth the Sun gives off, including the sunshine on your face.

cards.fact: The Sun holds about 99.8% of the solar system's mass.
cards.context: Every planet, moon, asteroid and comet together makes up the other 0.2%. NASA puts it this way: if the Sun were as tall as a front door, Earth would be about the size of a nickel. That enormous mass is why the Sun is in charge. Its gravity holds the solar system together and keeps every planet in its orbit.

cards.headline: Middle-aged, not old
cards.body: The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago. That sounds ancient, but a star like ours can fuse hydrogen for about 10 billion years, so the Sun is only around halfway through its life. There's plenty of hydrogen left in its core to keep it shining steadily for billions of years to come.
